utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm not sure why that signal indicates that we are in private session. I take it we are in open session. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. Mr. President, when we -- as we were adjourning the other day, the Trial Chamber asked if the Prosecution would address the Defence motion for a modification of segregation regime first thing this morning, and I'm prepared to do so now if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no basis for granting this motion. First, the motion itself states that there is no reason why Dr. Karadzic should not be able to have contact with Mr. Martic. That reflects a failure to review the order and the reasons given for the order that remains in -- that remains under seal, so I won't refer to it directly, but let me say more generically that it is a fairly conventional and time honoured prophylactic measure to impose some measure of segregation to avoid the possibility of interference or improper communications between an accused and certain witnesses in this case. This is a witness who was convicted for his participation in a joint criminal enterprise which involved the accused, so the basis for imposing restriction under such circumstances should be fairly clear. I am not aware that there is any jurisprudence suggesting that such segregation is in any way impermissible and the Defence has suggested none. Now, this order was made in early January, and now, approximately two months later, we see this motion which is clearly a motion for reconsideration which in no way attempts to address the standards for reconsideration. I want to be clear that I'm not suggesting that there should be an insurmountable standard for motions for reconsideration. Clearly if mistakes are made under appropriate circumstances, they should be remedied, but here the point is there is no attempt to even acknowledge the standard much less attempt to show how the Defence motion satisfies that standard. Instead, two things are suggested in passing, basically. One, that Dr. Karadzic has not been segregated from other -- all other detainees, and two, that the Prosecution has been free to have contact with its witnesses at any time except during their testimony. With respect to the first, Mr. President, given the ambitious nature of the Defence witness list, the accused would have to be in virtual isolation to segregate him from every person on his list, I would suggest, and it appears that for those persons who -- from whom he was not initially segregated after the witness list came out was obviously a somewhat idle gesture to impose it at that time. And in any event, it does not serve the Defence to argue that an imperfect system should be made more imperfect simply because logistical aspects make it difficult. It's clearly a different situation imposed on the Registry's attempt to balance the interests and the Trial Chamber's attempt when there's a temporary detainee coming in from outside. And in any event, here the Registry was responding to a direct order from the Court. And finally, with respect to the assertion about the Prosecution being free to have contact, the Defence team is also free to have contact. This is not a measure imposed on Dr. Karadzic as counsel, this is a measure imposed on him as an accused and it does not apply to the remainder of the trial team. There is no impermissible or improper segregation being imposed with respect to the teams, and this is a misleading characterization. So for those reasons, Mr. President, I would submit that there is no basis for this motion, and it should be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. I'm actually very surprised to hear the Prosecution's position because we didn't interfere or attempt to take any positions when it was deciding how it could meet its witnesses and prepare its witnesses. In fact, if you think of Momir Nikolic, who was also detained at the UNDU, I'm sure he was pulled out of his cell at least 20 times, if not more, so that the OTP could meet with him during the course of his detention and the course of his preparation for testimony. So I think it's a little incongruous for the Prosecution, first of all, even to be taking a position about how the Defence can access its witnesses, and secondly, to take one that's completely contrary to its own practice with its witnesses. So the reason that we believe that this motion is well founded is because there's simply no logical reason for a restriction on Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Martic meeting before his testimony, and any restrictions ought to be proportional to the aim at which they're directed. And the aim here is to avoid interference with a witness who is going to give testimony, and that applies when the witness starts his testimony. That's how it applies to the Prosecution, and that's how it applies to the Defence. And so we don't mind that kind of segregation once the testimony starts, but there's no logical reason why Dr. Karadzic can't meet with Mr. Martic on any other occasions. And so in the absence of any logical reason for the restriction, we don't think that it ought to be maintained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. General Vasiljevic, probably you will be well aware of this, but before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of evidence that we have at this Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read a short summary of General Vasiljevic's statement in the English language. [In English] Aleksandar Vasiljevic is a retired general from the Yugoslav Army, VJ. From 1986 to 1998, General Vasiljevic was the chief of the counter-intelligence service within the Department of Security of Federal Secretariat for People's Defence. In 1988, he was commander of division in Sarajevo where he stayed until July 1990. From 15th of June, 1991, to May the 8th, 1992, General Vasiljevic was the head of the Department for Security. In May 1992, General Vasiljevic retired. He was reactivated on 7th of April, 1999, and he became deputy chief of the security department of VJ. As chief of the counter-intelligence service, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic's job was to uncover foreign intelligence services, intelligence activity against the JNA and the army and to uncover the activities of the Yugoslav enemy emigration. In addition to -- in addition, he was to uncover enemy activities within the JNA. In this role, he uncovered Croatian separatist groups within the JNA as well as Albanian separatist organisations who tried to carry out several terrorist operations including poisoning of food of soldiers and officers. Further, a significant number of foreign intelligence agencies were discovered in Yugoslavia, and following Tito's death, there was a rise of nationalist tensions which the foreign services exploited, supporting separatist movements. General Vasiljevic considers that as early as in the mid-'80s [sic] the Croats armed themselves illegally and with a large number of weapons. They created their illegal army, which they later renamed to law enforcement officers when they were uncovered. All that time they were arming their HDZ party illegally, and advocated the killing of JNA and Serbs on their doorsteps regardless of age or gender. The Croatian authorities had prepared everything to create a Serbian camp. When this information became public, this caused a general uprising and revolt among the Serbs. The state of SFRY was unable to prevent these events because it had to order the army to disarm all these formations and arrest all rebels. The Serbs in Croatia, therefore, had no other choice but to organise themselves in order to protect themselves. The JNA did not try to protect Serbs in Croatia, merely prevent clashes between the two ethnic groups. Serbs did not have paramilitary organisations. In the second half of 1990, HDZ, Croatian party, had control in Western Herzegovina, which the authorities of BH were aware of. Despite Aleksandar Vasiljevic's request not to involve BH in the war, Croatia tried to get Bosnia and Macedonia involved at all costs. In July 1991, the first reports of the SDA, Muslim party in Bosnia, military organisation in the Doboj sector of BH were received. Military training had begun in Croatia, which then spread to Sarajevo. However, there were no hard facts. Sometime in mid-September, information was passed to General Vasiljevic that the Patriotic League was being formed from SDA headquarters and that three or four officers had left the army and joined them. There were regional offices for the Patriotic League in Serbia and part of Montenegro and there existed both military and political staff at every level. The Patriotic League began to block roads and JNA facilities. The Patriotic League was financed through exchanges of old Croatian money, in which -- as a matter Yugoslav money that was in Croatia, in which the Patriotic League would take half of the amount of exchange. This money was used to buy weapons from the Croats. In early 1991, the SDA began to make defence plans and preparing for secession and joining Croatia. Radovan Karadzic issued an order that Serbs should not provide Muslims and Croats with an excuse to attack. The SDA conducted raids to obtain more weapons from the Patriotic League -- for the Patriotic League. JNA operations were disrupted, attacks carried out on military organs, and secretariats for national defence in municipalities were broken into and records set on fire. The Patriotic League opened fire upon two wounded Serbs. To prevent escalation, Serbs were reminded not to retaliate, and they remained passive. Pleas were made in the JNA to stop Bosnia being dragged into the war as the Croats were moving troops through Bosnia. Some JNA troops were mobilised which was met with some resistance from the troops in Croatia and between 12 and 15 soldiers were killed. A number of Muslims left the JNA and a large number of Serbian volunteers and -- filled their places. In October 1991, joint check-points with the BH MUP were established to secure five bridges, and this action postponed the war in Bosnia by six months. However, these types of actions were not possible in Croatian part of Herzegovina. Roadblocks in the area were set up and heavy and anti-aircraft weapons appeared in Western Herzegovina where the HDZ were well armed. The charitable society Merhamet was used by the SDA Crisis Staff for paramilitary organisation of its members. In December 1991, further weapons were distributed to the Patriotic League from the chief of the MUP of police. In early 1992, the Serbs did not have a military staff. They did not have people making plans or a structure of the units, and they did not issue orders to attack the JNA units. The JNA were supported by the Serbs as people responded to the call-up and the mobilisation, recording -- reporting for compulsory military service and did not block the JNA army barracks or attack JNA members and their families. After a joint meeting at the BH MUP on 19th of January, 1992, it was agreed that paramilitary units should be disbanded. However, this was not done because there was no political will by any of the military leaders to publicly issue a call to their people to lay down their weapons. The service wrote a report to the SFRY Presidency about the situation and proposed that the Presidency declare a state of emergency. However, this was returned without an option about the measures proposed. At a meeting with Izetbegovic, General -- of General Vasiljevic, he denied -- Izetbegovic denied knowledge of the SDA paramilitary organisations and refused to communicate with Milosevic, the Serbian leadership, or to preserve Yugoslavia, but he did promise that as long as it was up to him, there would be no attack on the army in Bosnia. Publicly, Izetbegovic denied having any knowledge of the Patriotic League. In March 1992, a Serbian wedding guest was killed in Bosnia, and the Muslims began to make public appearance in Patriotic League uniforms. Barricades were erected and despite the efforts of the service these remained standing. The situation worsened as the Green Berets opened fire on a military police patrol and entered flats of military servicemen searching for weapons. During March, there were a number of skirmishes between the military and the paramilitary units. Fighting broke out in Bijeljina and was the first armed conflict between Serbs and Muslims and the first serious clash as a bomb was thrown to -- at the cafe where Serbs and Muslims gathered. Cafes, two cafes. The SDA carried out planned attack during April 1992, killing officers, seizing weapons, raiding a number of premises, blocking JNA premises, disarming soldiers, and spreading misinformation. Many further attacks occurred in the Serbs -- or on the Serbs despite the talks of withdrawal. These were not successful. The Republika Srpska military security arrested the Zute Ose, Yellow Wasps, and turned them over to the Bijeljina MUP for killings committed. Relations between Serbs and JNA were complex. The JNA assisted local commanders in BH if requested. The JNA was attacked as the enemy by the SDA, but the JNA continued to assist the Serbs by arming them with -- when they could. The JNA was a guarantor of peace. The Serbs sent recruits and reserves to the JNA as they did not have their own military organisation. Co-operation between the army and the BH MUP was supported by the Serbs, check-points were set up to control the territory and assist in disarming. And that would be the very short summary of this significant statement, and I do not have questions for General Vasiljevic at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one quick question for Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson. In paragraph 218, it refers to 1D55. We -- that we admitted just now, but it refers to a JNA warehouse, but looking at the document, I don't see any comment about JNA warehouse. If you could clarify that issue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, by your leave, I just need some time to have it clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload 1D55. Or if you are minded to withdraw that exhibit, we'll just proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we have withdrawn far too many documents. In other words, this is an invaluable witness, and we can lead hundreds of documents through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what the command of the 741st DOP is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is the command of the 741st Replenishment Regiment located in Travnik. Within their area of responsibility, there was a warehouse of JNA weapons and ammunition cache in Slimena. At that warehouse there was an attack on the 5th of April by members of the HOS, which was a Croatian paramilitary force, and the Patriotic League. 31 soldiers were taken prisoner and one officer at the warehouse. The HOS members executed two soldiers by firing squad on the site and the rest of the soldiers were taken to their military prison in Ljubuski, whereas 10 soldiers were left in the hands of Muslims. DOP doesn't stand for any volunteer unit, but it was an establishment unit called Replenishment Regiment. It was a kind of reserve unit as part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So in paragraph 218, it shouldn't say "KOS" but "HOS," H-O-S?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, does this answer your question about the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether this document refers to either that JNA warehouse or the attack against it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, as the General just explained. He explained the acronyms used in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this document refers to what General just has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I see your point, because this document is referring to the Territorial Defence depot at Slimena. So perhaps Dr. Karadzic can ask the witness what the connection is between that depot and the JNA warehouse referred to in paragraph 218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The General has heard what Mr. Robinson has said. Can you assist us as regards this document you are looking at on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could someone please put the volume up for me to hear interpretation. If I understood properly, I need to explain what the link is between the 741st Replenishment Regiment and the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The warehouse which is allegedly to be TO depot at Slimena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was a JNA warehouse under the authority of the command of the -- of the 741st Replenishment Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General, do you see the document in front of you? In the first paragraph it refers to the TO depot, Territorial Defence depot, at Slimena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Slimena a part of the weapons could have been that had been withdrawn from the TO by virtue of an order of the chief of the General Staff from 1989. This is a daily report drafted by the commander of the Replenishment Regiment describing the situation on that day. Some pressure is being exerted by members of the HOS and Muslims, primarily members of the Patriotic League, to have the weapons distributed to them as well so that they wouldn't be left without any. So the Slimena warehouse was a military warehouse where part of the TO weapons were probably located following their withdrawal in 1989 by the order of the Chief of the General Staff. However, it was not a TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Since this has been already admitted, I'll leave it at that, but, Mr. Karadzic, in the future, when you are tendering documents as part of associated exhibit, be cautious whether they form indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. General Vasiljevic, as you have noted that your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, i.e., through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, first of all, I wish to thank you for participating in an interview with the Prosecution last week, and I will address some of the topics that we discussed during the interview in the course of the cross-examination, and as we have to cover quite some topics and very little time, I kindly ask you to just answer the questions as precisely as possible and not add matters that I didn't ask you about. Otherwise, I will have to interrupt you, and I would not like to do that. General, in paragraph 32 of your statement, you said that in the relevant time, the JNA was the fourth strongest army in Europe, and in paragraph 70 you -- you stated, referring to the situation in March 1991, you said that the army did not burst at ethnic seams. General, at that time you were proud of being a JNA officer; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is right, and I'm still proud for having been a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you saw the JNA as a multi-ethnic army with a mission to protect the multi-ethnic Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you were retired on the 8 of -- 8th of May, 1992, together with 38 other generals, although the conditions for your retirement were not met; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those retiring you at that time were opposed to your view of the multi-ethnic concept of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Partially correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, you said the following: You speak of the general climate of discrimination at that time, that there was an ethnic cleansing of the army of those who were not born in Serbia and Montenegro, and you gave the example of Deputy Tumanov, and that you also said that General Panic scolded you for still having some Croats in your service.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I refer here to the -- to the Slobodan Milosevic testimony of the General, and it is uploaded under 65 ter 22492, and I was referring to the e-court pages 306 through 308, and e-court page 589.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, that -- that captures the situation, how it was in spring 1992, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in the beginning of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, the JNA acted as a buffer army between the two sides, but that changed in the course of the year 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The general principle in the JNA did not change. However, much depended on the movements of certain local commanders in the field who deviated from the positions provided by the SSNO, the Federal Secretariat of All People's Defence. So in the field there were occasions where they supported local forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have document P02601 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, and as it is coming up, it is a cover letter by Major General Polic of the 9th Corps Command of the JNA, and if we go to the next page, it is enclosing the directive -- on both pages, please. It's enclosing the directive of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence on the use of the armed forces of the 10th of October, 1991. General, I assume you are familiar with this directive.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was not on the 10th of October but on the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I misspoke. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 in both languages, and we have to focus on the top part. And -- in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it says here: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war: protection of the Serbian population ..." and so on and so forth. General, the JNA at that time was no longer a buffer, no longer protecting all peoples, but, rather, protecting the Serbs, at least according to this directive, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is December 1991, it means that the war in Croatia had ended by that time and Slovenia had seceded. Not -- by not honouring any procedure, Croatia had seceded as well from the then Yugoslavia and the JNA was put in a new position as compared to the period before the 15th of September when there were military attacks of the Croatian armed forces on the JNA, when the war broke out between Croatia and the JNA. So this is late 1991 when the directive was drafted. It was decided that people be protected from terror and destruction. Those people who disagreed with living outside of Yugoslavia, those who were denied their right to enjoy the same privilege as the other people as to choose where to live. The Serb people refused to live in the seceded banana states and it opted for remaining in Yugoslavia. Since it was contrary to the policy in place in Croatia at the time, they were supposed to be protected from persecution and the conflict between the autonomous regions which had been constituted at the time. The JNA, in other words, was protecting the Serb population that was in danger. It doesn't mean that it persecuted others who lived in Serbia. You know well that Serbia is a multinational state, and neither Croats nor any other ethnicities had problems with remaining there and living there as they had before. I see nothing that would be disputed in this directive. By your leave, since I recall it particularly well, although you asked me not to go off on a tangent, but the directive also deals with the issue of dealing with paramilitary and volunteer formations once wartime activities have been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General. I actually wanted to move on to this topic, and if you go to page 4 in both languages, under point 6 -- under point 6 it says: "In all zones of combat operations, place under command of the most senior JNA officer all units of the JNA and TO as well as volunteer units ..." and so on and so forth. And, General, that is what you just referred to, this principle of unified command; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this principle continued also in Bosnia, and it was also applied by the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: One needs to distinguish between the TO and -- well, I've already testified about it in the Milosevic case. In Slavonia and Srem, there were two TOs in my view. There was the legal TO and a local TO established by the new authorities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was only one TO. So it had not been divided into two, at least not until late March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But here in this particular order when it refers to the JNA and the TO, it was basically the Serb TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the TO of the independent or autonomous region of Western Srem and Baranja. Let me remind you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, General. I have to interrupt you because we have to move on. If we need more details, I will tell you. But here the Serb TO in that area and later also in Bosnia, they were considered friendly force and co-operating with the JNA while the Croat and the Muslim TOs were not; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb TO, as you define it, never attacked the JNA. The Muslim and Croat TOs were objectively paramilitary formations by definition, and they attacked the JNA. Neither of the TOs, although I underscore the difference between the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the TO in Krajina and the Sirmium or the Srem region. As for the Patriotic League, as what was to become the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, they killed our first officers in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 5th of April, 1992, in the village of Sapna, for no reason at all, a military police patrol was attacked when warrant officer Mihajlo Stanojevic was killed and two reserve sergeants as well as four soldiers out of the ten that were there. For no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I mean, we have all these details in written form already before the Court, so we do not need to repeat this. I would like to -- to move on now and referring to armed Serbs. You have mentioned armed Serbs in your statement, and I refer here to paragraphs 88 and 113. General, the JNA or, rather, elements thereof armed the Serb TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is right if we address it as an occurrence or a relationship as of March 1992. Let me remind you of the fact that the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, objectively speaking, was broken up because the reserve part of the TO which comprised Muslims and Croats, simply did not respond to any call-ups to replenish the units of the TO, the legitimate TO headed by Drago Vukosavljevic, a JNA general. So the manning levels in units went down because Alija Izetbegovic called on all Bosniaks and Muslims to leave the army, and they prevented any new recruits being sent to serve their military term in the JNA. The JNA did not have appropriate manning levels at the time. The manning levels were raised by some TO ranks which by that time one could refer to as the Serb TO, but until the 8th of April, 1992, it existed as the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not a paramilitary unit. Some TO units were simply drafted. They were mobilised. In the conflict in Croatia, there were some Serbian TO units that were mobilised and sent to the area of Srem. I discussed them, for example, the Smederevo TO detachment, the Palanka TO detachment, et cetera. Those were legal TO units. However, your question was whether there were instances where someone from the JNA armed the so-called Serb TO as you call it. There were such instances, and I can cite an example where we raised a criminal report against a major who issued weapons to local Serbs without any approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, General --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is why --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: May I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Let's -- let's go step-by-step. One of these officers who provided weapons to what I call the Bosnian Serb TO, and you call it differently, was General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to a document that you basically know about from your testimony in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's here -- Your Honour, it's here P05431.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, when you -- it should be -- yeah. And when you see it coming up, you will remember it because you also discussed it in the Milosevic case. It's a report of the 1st kk to the Main Staff of the VRS concerning the control and issuance of weapons to the TO staffs dated 31st August 1992, and when we move to the next page, please, we basically see a list of items being provided. It's a lengthy list of items. You remember this particular document, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I said then that this is a document from August 1992. It was a period when I had already retired. That was the period when the Army of Republika Srpska was established as a legal army, and it has to do with the requests when TO units were being established in accordance with the Vance Plan. And especially in Krajina the TO units were manned and they went to depots that were under lock and key. It says here that in the period when the army was established, because I cannot see when the weapons were issued. This is from the month of August. They had to sign for it and then it had to be returned eventually. So I do not see anything strange about it. This was the moment when the Army of Republika Srpska came into being, and it is my duty to recall, though you said -- you will say that you haven't asked me that, that there was an order of the chief of General Staff, General Blagoje Adzic who said that no equipment or weapons must be issued to any TO unit or anyone else unless this was verified at the level of the General Staff. So it was not just chaotic distribution of weapons any old how, but it was a lawful and organised distribution of weapons to the units that were supposed to provide protection of the rear in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But your understanding of this document, if we go back to the first page, is not that those items were all provided in -- on the 31st of August, but, rather, it's a -- it's a document referring to what had been done until the 31st of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you do know that from the 19th of May, there was no more JNA, and in Bosnia, the Army of Republika Srpska had been constituted and General Mladic was appointed commander of that army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's -- let's move on. General, during the interview that we had last week, you confirmed that you were aware that certain JNA officers would co-operate with the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that on that -- through this way Serbs got weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: You are partly correct. You asked me then when we talked, just as you're asking me today, whether some officers co-operated with the SDS. The answer I gave was along the following lines, that we had certain JNA officers who were being disciplined because they had expressed some kind of nationalism, Serb, Croat, et cetera, whereas those officers whose names had been mentioned had not co-operated with the SDS. Before the SDS had been constituted, they had expressed extreme Serb nationalist positions. Again, I have to be rather extensive in order to paint a clear picture for you. When I was in Sarajevo on the 23rd of April, 1992, with regard to reaching agreement on when Alija Izetbegovic would meet with General Blagoje Adzic and Branko Kostic, then the security officers briefed me about the security situation in their areas of responsibility, and, inter alia, they told me that the SDS headquarters were moved to Pale. There is not a single officer active-duty member of the JNA who is with them in their headquarters. There is no a single officer who moved there with them. We had no officers in these SDS staffs, whereas we do have Muslim officers who actually constituted the Patriotic League. So one officer, I can even give you the name if necessary, he was a major, he established contact with people from the top echelons of the SDS, and that is why criminal charges were brought against him and then he fled and he became a wanted man. That's only case we had of that kind. Also, in Tuzla we had officers who held these extremist positions, and this colonel contacted some Chetnik formations. Not with the SDS committee in Tuzla but with the Chetnik units that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you also confirmed during our talks last week that in fact the majority of the Serb JNA officers originating from Bosnia supported the SDS because they had the same objective, namely, first staying in Yugoslavia and later on having their own Serb republic or entity in Bosnia. That was the general position at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you keep linking that to the SDS, and this actually has to do with one's attitude towards the Serbian issue as such and towards what had been happening in Yugoslavia over the preceding year. They thought that when various peoples expressed their wish where they wanted to live and went their own way, they thought that the Serbs also had the right to decide on where they wanted to live. They did not want to live seceded in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they thought that their place was in Yugoslavia. They wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. Whether that was SDS policy, I don't know. However, it does not mean that these officers were linked to the SDS. I kindly ask you to accept that, because I know what the situation was in the JNA. We have Serb nationalists. We have extremists who believe that Serbs are exploited, that they're subjugated like all other peoples who had -- held such beliefs and that were manipulated in that way. However, this doesn't have to do with links between officers and the SDS. That is why I presented that information of the 23rd of April, when the chief of security briefed me stating that there was not a single officer who went with the SDS to Pale or to some military staff if they had one, and I was not aware of them having one to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you already mentioned that you investigated and disciplined certain officers for their extreme nationalist behaviour, and as I remember our talks, in relation to the Sarajevo Corps, that is, the JNA force corps, you had actually four officers investigated, colonels, that is; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation is not correct that I carried out an investigation. An investigation is carried out when there is evidence or suspicion of the commission of a crime. I was a security officer. We did not carry out investigations. It was the SUP that carried out the investigation. We carried out different operative measures at different levels to a different extent vis-a-vis persons for whom we believed that they were expressing views from the viewpoint of Serbian nationalism. It's not true that they were all in the 4th Corps, the Sarajevo Corps. This corps came into being in its real form only after I left the position of division commander. Some of them were in the 4th Motorised Division and others were in the 4th Corps that existed then. However, if you're speaking about 1992, March, April, it is correct that all of these officers were in the 4th Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? I wanted to intervene. This misunderstanding stems from line 18, page 26. The General said that they were being processed, not disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned among those four was a Colonel Gagovic, and you said he's a Montenegrin, and you couldn't remember the first name. Do you now remember the first name? You wanted to think about it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really think about it, but I seem to remember now that it's Milosav Gagovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did he at that time deal with logistics in the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's at the time when I was commander of the division in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to move on to something that you already touched upon, and we need to see 65 ter 01726. And as it is coming up, General, it is an order from the command of the 2nd Military District, dated 9 January 1992, regarding an earlier order on the procedure from the SSNO dated the 31st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. Or rather, wait, wait. Can we first look -- let's have the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at the preamble and point 1 of the order, this order enforces the procedure to be applied for the equipment of TO units with weapons and equipment. That's what the preamble says.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the underlying order, the underlying order is on the next, page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You -- you refer to this order in your statement already at paragraph 207, and you have already touched upon it here. The reason why the TO units are now requested not to contact the SSNO directly, but, rather, go through the command of the JNA units in which zone they are located, that's because they had so many requests suddenly to deal with at the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the end of 1991. This is a period when preparations are being carried out for the demilitarisation of the Knin Krajina. Territorial Defence units are being formed in the Knin Krajina, and equipment and weapons are being provided -- are being sent to the warehouse, and there is this joint key that is used to lock them. That includes the international forces, and this does not pertain only to the units of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina because this is procedure related to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say that Kukanjac had not only Bosnia-Herzegovina under his command but also part of the Krajina. But this also pertained to the Territorial Defence units of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were supposed to be constituted, and in the documentation that was shown, and I believe that you will find that now, too, you will see about the constitution of the special MUP detachment in Banja Luka and they're asking the military to give them two helicopters, two military helicopters. This is megalomaniac requests. This is not illegal. These are not paramilitaries. These are legal units of the Territorial Defence that were primarily constituted on the basis of the Vance Plan in the area of the Krajina and they were supposed to be demilitarised, whereas the JNA was pulled out from that area into Bosnia as a guarantee that the Serbs would not be attacked after that. So this document pertains partly to Krajina and partly to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, you have already referred to this, as you call it, megalomaniac order or request.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have a look at it. It is 65 ter 01713.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up here, it is General Kukanjac, on 24th April 1992, is forwarding and endorsing a request of the Ministry of Interior of the Serb Republic for a huge number of weapons, equipment and, as you said, helicopters even. That is what you just referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's already the 24th of April. Not to say that two days after that, there was an oral agreement between General Adzic and Alija Izetbegovic concerning the fate of the JNA, the division of the JNA, leaving equipment and weaponry and so on, and then these megalomaniac requests come in as to what they would get from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was taken up to the highest level in order to keep under control what would happen with JNA weapons and equipment once the JNA withdraws.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. General, you have to speak a bit more slowly. The interpreters didn't catch part of what you said, but I think the answer is translated -- is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's already in evidence as Exhibit P5432.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in your statement you focus on the activities of the Muslims. The arming of the Serbs and their activities was not a priority for you in your work because the -- as you said, the Serbs were supporting the JNA and the focus, therefore, was on the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I focused on the problem that was against the JNA. Had the Serbs organised themselves through paramilitaries and had they attacked the JNA, then they would have been processed by JNA organs. So we did not focus on the Muslims because they were Muslims and the Serbs were on the other side. What we discovered was a paramilitary organisation whose activity was aimed against the JNA. In my explanation of the introduction of this operative action that had to be approved by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, I refer to the parameters why it is the military that has to deal with these services. Serbs did not threaten us. I did not have security-related problems with the Serbs, and we applied measures from the scope of our legislative -- legal powers because Serbs were not working against us. Croats weren't, and Muslims weren't either, but their paramilitaries did work against the JNA and that's why I took action. I assume that I've been speaking too fast again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During your interview that we had last week, you said that the -- the Serbs and the SDS considered the JNA to be their army basically. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the sense that they were the owners and commanders of the army but that it was their army, just as the JNA used to be the army of all the peoples of Yugoslavia. So that was that in that sense, but it's not that they commanded it or took it upon themselves to act as if it were only their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you have already referred to a meeting between General Adzic and President Izetbegovic and other persons, including members of the SFRY Presidency on the 26th of April, 1992, in Skopje, and it's also referred to in your statement, and we indeed have a transcript of an audio recording of this meeting that I would like to discuss with you next.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 11020 on the screen. And let's -- sorry. And let's just move into the text, page 3 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have here Mr. Izetbegovic proposes that the elements of the Yugoslav Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be transformed as of tomorrow into the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a bit further down under point 2, that the armed forces must accept the authority of the civil government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a bit further down, next paragraph, that the composition of the command personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be changed as well as the next -- as it says in the next paragraph, the troops. General, you were aware of this position that Izetbegovic took; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I read this document here, the one that's been displayed just now. I don't know who wrote it up and who authorised it -- or, rather, who authored it, because there are certain interruptions and ambiguities. When I say "interruptions," they interrupt the negotiations for lunch and then they continue after that. And I did not see how it continued, and usually people agree on a lot of things over lunch. I know about this interpretation of General Blagoje Adzic on the 27th of April, in Belgrade, when he briefed the General Staff about what they had agreed upon, and that was a preliminary agreement. I can say what I know from that oral briefing, because there were many options there that were being looked at. One was that the JNA would stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it had to be harmonised with the ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there are different options that are bandied about. So I don't see from this what it was that was ultimately agreed upon. I know what General Adzic told us about when he returned, though. The first and basic thing was with regard to the fate of the army. General Blagoje Adzic advocated the following: That the JNA should stay until the peace forces arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, guaranteeing a peaceful resolution of the Bosnian crisis. A position was taken that was allegedly agreed upon by both sides that all of those who were not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and were within the JNA would leave Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 19th. All of those who are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are in the JNA in some other areas would be duty-bound to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina by that dead-line. Retired military personnel were guaranteed equal rights as if they had been pensioned off in the JNA. However, in terms of the division of the remaining equipment and weaponry from the JNA, a multi-disciplinary commission was supposed to be set up as was done in Skopje when the army was leaving Macedonia. That was supposed to be agreed upon during May 1992. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, General, let me interrupt you here, because we do not have this transcript of the section that was after the lunch. We only have this one, and I would like to stick with this one for a few more minutes, because what you have said what the agreement is actually in your written evidence. I was wondering only about Mr. Izetbegovic's concerns about the ethnic composition of the JNA at that time, and he basically states here on this page that it was -- had been upset and should be restored to reflect the ethnic composition of the population. And if I understand you correctly, he is right here. The -- the JNA had become sort of a Serb army at that time. Most of the personnel were Serb, of Serb ethnicity; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say again that it is not so. First of all, it did not become a Serb army, because not all the Muslims left the JNA by the 19th of May. I have specific data; namely, that by the 31st of January, 1992, a total of 317 Muslim officers had left the JNA, of which 65 had not done it in a lawful way. So they were treated as military deserters. And we had 69 Muslim officers who reported to the security organs, the appearance of the Muslim paramilitary formations which tried to win them over. So it is not true that the JNA was left without any Muslims by that time. What Mr. Izetbegovic did not mention at the meeting was that the 2nd Military District as the highest military command in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have any Muslim generals. There was Muharem Fetahagic who hails from Kumanovo -- or, rather, was transferred from Kumanovo to Bosnia precisely for the reason that he would be a Muslim general in the army. Another general who was a Muslim was wounded in Dobrovoljacka Street. I will try to remember his last name. He used to be in 51st Brigade. Then for a while the commander of the 4th Corps used to be a Croat, a general who later on left the JNA and went away. So what you emphasise is only one segment. Blagoje Adzic responded to them then in this text. I can see it. What would it be like? You have caused the JNA to be composed mainly of Serbs, because by your calls from August 1991, you invited Muslims not to respond to call-ups. You prohibited the Muslims from serving the JNA. So you caused this composition of the JNA. So he asked: How can you now request that a Muslim be appointed the commander of this, conditionally speaking, Serbian Army? It would be the same as if I would request from you to appoint me as the commander of your Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me -- let me --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: So this is all something that can be seen from the discussion. I have read it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let us move to page 9 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do it after the break, if it is convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 5 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, we were just -- before the break we spoke about the composition of the JNA in Bosnia at that time, and let's move to English page 9 in the document and page 13 in the B/C/S, and then we can see what General Adzic says about that point. And General Adzic speaks of several tens of thousands troops and states that the JNA is mainly filled with personnel from Bosnia-Herzegovina, with over 80 per cent of them coming from that territory and over 90 per cent of them being Serbs living there. General, what the SSNO says here, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it's correct. I do not have the figures that testify to the strength of the JNA. It is strange, though, that he speaks precisely how many people there are in the TO, 35.000 in the Serbian TO, and then about the Croats, and then he says several tens of thousands in the Muslim TO. He should have said precisely how many there were. Personally, I don't think that there were several tens of thousands of JNA members in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this is his statement, so I cannot comment on it, and I'm not aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just leaving aside the numbers, whether you remember them and whether General Adzic is right here, but these JNA personnel that were -- that were at that time in Bosnia and were coming, originating, from Bosnia, they were transformed into the VRS when it was created, except of course those that were unwilling or, rather -- and, rather, left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 22 in the English, and it is starting on page 32 -- sorry, yes, 32 in the B/C/S and goes over into page 33 and even page 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Izetbegovic is again speaking, and he's referring to strong paramilitary organisations of the SDS having its control -- having under its control quite a number of territories, and he speaks of Bijeljina, Foca, Samac, and the surroundings of Sarajevo. By that time, 26th of April, General, would that be correct? Did the Serbs control quite a huge territory by then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that they had control in the places which are mentioned here, that means Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Visegrad, but not in the entire territory. He talks about the towns in which a conflict with the Patriotic League broke out between the Serbian population and the Patriotic League and the forces that were infiltrated from Serbia, but I'm not aware of the fact that they controlled the entire territory along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 19 of your statement, you refer to the time that parties with mostly national prefixes became legal, and giving your, let's put it, multi-ethnic views on how the country should continue, that was a disturbance, right, having these national parties giving speeches, inflaming the populations? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone was doing it from their own position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just please ask whether the General has his statement available, and can he check it when the Prosecution quotes specific paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, but I didn't quote anything from a paragraph. I only mentioned that in paragraph 19, he spoke about -- he referred to parties with mostly nationalist prefixes became legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue, but I don't see any difficulty with providing the witness with his statement. Can you print one in the meantime in B/C/S. You'll have it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't bring it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in your testimony in the Milosevic case - and I refer here to e-court page 510 - you said the following: "There was a spectre of ethnic passions fanned in all environments. Rather than stopping the passions and hostilities, political authorities fanned them. The pattern was that the other ethnic group was blamed for something that had been done, whereas one's own people were, in the interpretation of the leaders, victims." General, that captures your observations during the events; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say all groups, this includes the SDS as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It's one thing when we talk about groups and another when we talk about parties. There were parties that were quite extreme. And as for the previous question, if you allow me to go back, you selected a specific part of my statement where I said that the parties mostly had ethnic prefixes, but as for extremes, I mentioned there that the HDZ brought extremists from the terrorist part of emigration who --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- then appeared at their convention in the Lisinski hall. So this is what I said previously, just to make a correction, even though I don't have the statement in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm sorry. General, I have to interrupt you, because that is what we actually have in writing already here, and I address things that are not already in evidence before this Court. So we don't need to repeat this. Thank you. But let's move on to the next topic and only briefly you have described in your statement, and I refer here to the paragraphs 130, 149, and 150, to several attempts of the security administration and the Bosnian police to get a grip on the arming of troops outside the JNA and how you co-operated, and we do not need to repeat it as it's all in writing. I just want to refer to a joint proposal of the security administration and the BiH MUP to disarm all paramilitary formations, and you refer in paragraph 157 to it, and you say the politicians did not support it, not in Bosnia and not on the federal level. That's how it was; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: As I cannot describe this extensively, one could not say that it was only the politicians who did not support this. Based on a meeting with the military leadership on the 24th of December, which was held with the Presidency of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had envisaged a plan of disarming all paramilitary formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 19th of January, we held a meeting. At the meeting, the representatives of MUP from Croatia, Bruno Stojic and Brano Kvesic who was head of the state security in Croatia obstructed this. They advocated that the people would not return the weapons and, if they were pressured to do so, that war would break out and that political parties should call on their peoples to return the weapons. And then an argument broke out between the representatives of the Serbs in the MUP and these Croats, and the meeting did not -- was not completed, and there was no plan to be applied as we had hoped. On the 5th of February, I went for talks with Alija Izetbegovic, because the previous attempt had failed. However, their interpretation was that political parties would not accept this. Whether they contacted between the 19th of January and the 5th of February when I came to Sarajevo again, whether they had contacts with their ethnic leaders, this is something I don't know, but it was obvious that generally speaking, no one wanted to accept it. The Presidency of SFRY did not react to this either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just say something about the transcript so that there would not be a confusion. General talked about the Croats in Bosnia rather than Croats from Croatia on T5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As we do not have much time, I move on now to another meeting, and we have no time to look at the document, but, General, you -- in your statement you mentioned that you met Mr. Izetbegovic as well as other Presidency members, and you may remember the meeting you had on the 15th of October, 1991, with all the members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is 65 ter 24661, but I think I don't need to pull it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In that meeting, non-Serb -- non-Serb members of the Presidency were concerned about what they called excessive high concentration of JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that, that that was a concern they had?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I inspected the document you talk about, which is entitled "Notes from the meeting." So much more was said than you just mentioned. There was interpretation as to why the number of troops in Bosnia increased, but what you just said is correct. But in any case, it is just an extract from that. If you wish to ask me about the following meeting which took place on the 24th of December, I already expressed my reserve about the way this meeting is interpreted. This is the key point. At that meeting, neither on the 15th of October or on the 24th, none of the Serbian representatives were present except for the members of the Presidency, Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic. Mr. Karadzic did not attend it, nor did Mr. Krajisnik. The first time I met Mr. Karadzic was when I came here. They did not attend this meeting, but during the discussion, even though he did not attend it, it says that he opposed the peacekeeping forces entering Bosnia. This is why I believe it is said that he attended the meeting, but the notes are not authentic, because persons who did not attend it are listed. And I never said anything at the meeting, because the principle is not for the subordinates to enter the discussion when you have the federal minister who is present. So the notes are untruthful, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your -- but as you said, you remember the meeting. The non-Serb members of the Presidency, they feared that the JNA would turn against them if they continue to pursue an independent Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not so. It wasn't that they were afraid that the army would turn against them. This is not noted there. I have my original notes from the -- from both meetings, and this was not expressed. We would have -- you will have to be more precise and tell me what the notes say. They were not afraid of the army. Alija Izetbegovic even asked the army to help to disarm the paramilitary formations, but he requested that paramilitary formations in Banja Luka also be disarmed. That was at the meeting of the 24th of December when they took over a relay owned by the TV and turned it in another direction. He was saying all the time what the Serbian side was doing and never mentioned the paramilitary formations which had already grown by that time and had an enormous amount of weapons. I don't know if you would ask me that or not, but there is something that is usually skipped over. As a former member of the Yugoslav People's Army, I care to say that the first victims, the first casualties in Bosnia-Herzegovina were military personnel, and in principle members of the military police. Let me give you the dates, the 18th of September, 1991, the 5th of April --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you -- General, I'm sorry, but we have only very limited time, and you have actually provided these details in the written statement. And I would like to move on so that we can cover one more topic where you can basically help us with, and that is the paramilitary units, irregular troops of all kind, and I want to discuss this with you as you have made observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 01718 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an order of the SFRY Presidency on the engagement of volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY during imminent threat of danger, dated 10 December 1991. I'm quite confident that you know this decision. Do you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw that decision here, because this is not the army Official Gazette but the Official Gazette of Serbia, and I read these provisions when I testified in the case against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And as it says here in paragraph 1, that "... during the imminent danger of war, the JNA and the TO are reinforced, among others, with volunteers who are from the moment they joined units and institutions of the armed forces of the SFRY, equal in all things with soldiers and military conscripts." General, there was a shortage of troops given the poor response to mobilisation at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this reinforcement with volunteers, that also occurred in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the volunteers or paramilitaries that you observed in Croatia would reappear, at least some of them would reappear in Bosnia, and I would just ask you about a few. The Yellow Wasps, they caused havoc in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And they were associated with Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have already given quite an extensive account of Arkan and his men in Bijeljina, and that's in your statement on paragraph 171 further. They were in Bijeljina. You said that already.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And your observations of such group -- troops in Croatia, from these observations you were aware that some of these volunteers and paramilitaries, and I include here Arkan, would loot, would mistreat the non-Serbs, and would even kill prisoners of war or innocent civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Arkan, you also mentioned in your testimony in Milosevic that his status in the field would shift constantly. At times he was part of the TO, sometimes police unit, and even on one occasion part of the Novi Sad Corps; right? You -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. He was never a member of the Novi Sad Corps, but the then-corps commander General Bijorcevic had direct links with him, but they were never a part of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Officially definitely not, as you have already mentioned also in the Milosevic case, but I seem to recall that you refer to an order you have seen where Arkan was basically named as a reconnaissance group of the Novi Sad Corps, but that was only a fiction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that General Bijorcevic not ordered him but sent him a memo claiming that in the area of Badovinci they were a reconnaissance group of the Novi Sad Corps, although they were not part of the Novi Sad Corps, nor did the other officers from the Novi Sad Corps know that Bijorcevic had issued them such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was referring to the e-court pages 62 to 63 from the Milosevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, Arkan's Tigers, as they were also called, were the dominant armed group taking part in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when we spoke last week, you mentioned that after the take-over of Bijeljina, Ms. Plavsic and the commander of the JNA Tuzla Corps met Arkan in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't just Ms. Plavsic who was there. There was also the commander of the Tuzla Corps, Djeneral Jankovic, then Fikret Abdic was there, as well as some other politicians who came as a delegation on behalf of Sarajevo to calm things down in Bijeljina. It is true that Ms. Plavsic was there and she greeted Arkan, kissing him on the cheeks when they met.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, if you look back at the observations you made regarding the events in Bosnia, would it be fair to say that crimes against the non-Serb people by Serb troops were tolerated by the political leaderships at certain times?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: What political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would -- I was actually referring to all political leaderships. But we can -- we can go and take one particular example. You are aware that the Yellow Wasps were arrested and later on set free; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know they were set free. It was probably after I retired. What I do know is this: Proceedings were instituted in Loznica, I believe, and one of them was released because he was not mentally fit to stand trial. He was held in the detention unit, though, after he was declared unfit. I think it occurred sometime later, in 1993 or 1994. I think that's when the trial took place. Recently, some people from that group were tried before the war crimes court in Belgrade, and I don't think all of the judgements have been handed down yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that Lukic was arrested and set free and then arrested again; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It all took place later, after I retired. However, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the Milosevic case - and I'm referring here, Your Honours, to page 284 in e-court - you, in fact, spoke about a modus operandi at that time to avoid prosecuting such perpetrators by transferring them back and forth over borders. Does that capture the prevailing attitude at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the prevailing attitude, but in both cases you mentioned, objectively speaking, that's what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have one -- yes. I have one more topic, and that's now an entirely different one, and it refers to paragraph 189, where you describe in the statement an event, an attack on the military depot near Foca on the 26th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to have D01683 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, as it is coming up, you refer in your -- in your statement to a military depot near Foca, and would that be the JNA fuel depot in Filipovici near Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have here a document from the 744th logistic base command, 17 April 1992, that refers to the situation in that area. Do you know this particular document? Have you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before we go into details, let me just understand whether I understood your comments properly. In paragraph 189, and if I understand the English translation correctly, is it your evidence that some of the Muslim refugees taking shelter there were armed, that they disarmed the JNA officers, and when the Serbs became aware of this, they attacked the depot and disarmed the Muslim attackers? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That's it more or less. Information was received through security organs to the extent that some 200 Muslims, refugees, took shelter in the warehouse. They were received there and fed. The decision to do so was made by Major Kurtovic, who was at the warehouse. Since some of the Muslims were armed, the personnel of the warehouse, including Kurtovic, were disarmed, and then an SDS unit became involved clearing up things. I have no further information, and what I state in the statement is what I have learned from the security organ. If you wish me to do so, I'll re-read it to see what happened indeed, or perhaps you can put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned now that the SDS units were indeed dealing with the situation at that time, and that's basically said here in this -- in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not already admitted as you indicated, D1683?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You're right. You're right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, we --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, there's also evidence before this Tribunal that - and I refer here to the adjudicated facts, Your Honour, 758 and 759 - that on the day of the attack on the warehouse by these SDS troops, nine Muslim men were murdered after an SDA membership card was found. General, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no -- no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You're not tendering 65 ter 1718, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which seems to be an SFRY Presidency order.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender it. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, only perhaps one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, in this indictment, I'm being charged with the following -- well, on page 27, you were asked about the positions of officers who supported the SDS. Did the JNA change its position about the SDS and supported it, or was it the SDS who suffered a change of heart and then supported the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any JNA position changing concerning the SDS. It simply did not engage in discussions with any political party.
