Now, whether the SDS changed their position vis-a-vis the JNA, well, I seem to remember something which was in early April, perhaps, when the SDS changed its position concerning the purpose of co-operating between the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the TO, and they justified it by having -- by the situation being changed. The MUP had split into the Serb and Muslim parts, so there was no purpose in further co-operating with the Muslim MUP. Until the last day of my service, we never changed our position on co-operating with the MUP. That is the only change I am aware of in terms of SDS position at the beginning, which was praised at all of the meetings. It was stated that the co-operation in question was a positive move which contributed to preserving peace in Bosnia for at least a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment, I am charged with supporting JNA draft calls. In your knowledge, does that amount to a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you would be charged with something the people were supposed to do anyway as citizens. There were some volunteers which were called that in the sense that they participated in the conflict in Croatia. That's how they were referred to in street parlance. In Croatia, there were two collection centres for volunteers at the beginning of the war which were soon disbanded because those volunteers would not remove their party insignia. In the conflict in Kosovo in 1999, we also had two collection centres for volunteers where in an organised fashion they were received. We did not establish such centres in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because people themselves, as per their war deployment, reported to JNA units, and the SDS called on their -- on its membership to honour their duty as citizens. I'm not saying that perhaps such volunteers did not form a paramilitary unit of their own, but those people arrived in the JNA of their own accord and were made part of the JNA. Since the truth seems not to be able to out here in terms of JNA -- the JNA in Bosnia, in addition to the volunteers who voluntarily joined the JNA, eight of them were executed by firing squad in the centre of Sarajevo in front of the police hall. They had been taken prisoner in Dobrinja and dragged out of an APC which had broken down. These were not actually volunteers but JNA soldiers who had been drafted from the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It is very good that you mention it. At page 46 you were asked whether you were aware that volunteers and paramilitary units which you had met in Croatia would engage in looting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can one put the sign of equation between a paramilitary formation and volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Those who reported in Croatia as volunteers were brought there by political parties through their rallies, and by that time they had set them up as some sort of military units which had not -- which did not make part of the JNA later on, but they moved under the name of this or that volunteer group. They had different names such as Dusan Silni, Leva Supoderica, and so on and so forth. The situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was completely different. There, there was general refusal to call-ups, and the 216th Mountain Brigade in Han Pijesak had only 33 per cent manning levels. In our army where -- where during exercises the reserves used to respond to such exercises in great numbers, if the percentage was less than 90 per cent, the commander was considered unsuccessful. There was a call to not to respond to call-ups in Bosnia-Herzegovina starting with Alija Izetbegovic and the Patriotic League, and in that case this brigade had the manning level of only 33 per cent. I was unaware of the Yellow Wasps during the conflict in Croatia. I heard of them for the first time concerning the Zvornik incident. As for Arkan's units, they were in Croatia. And I cannot put the sign of equation between volunteers and paramilitaries. Paramilitary units had already been established and those groups moved about the theatre. Even in Kosovo they attempted to insert a paramilitary group of 25 headed by some Jugoslav Petrusic. They circumvented the collection centres for volunteers. Ninety per cent of those who reported to the collection centres were eliminated as unfit to join the army due to their previous conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you observe that someone could report as a volunteer and, later on, to cut himself loose, creating a paramilitary unit and refusing to adhere to JNA regulation -- regulations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: If someone chose to go maverick, that person was an individual. It was not a group and as such would be considered a military deserter. That person would have to be bring in because they had been members of the regular army. I don't know of such cases in Bosnia-Herzegovina out of the people who responded to the call-up to wartime units. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last question, General: You mentioned that you had several officers in Sarajevo who were being processed or investigated, and it was misinterpreted as if you had disciplined them. The processing you mentioned, did it manage to prove that, for example, Colonel Gagovic had committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Only Gagovic was mentioned in that context. Although we are not in closed session, I can tell you that there were a few dozen investigations or processing procedures conducted by security organs at the time on different elements of their responsibility or liability that fell within the remit of security organs. There were several investigations conducted on the topic of Serb nationalism. As far as I know, Gagovic was not connected to any person from the SDS. As far as I know, he was appointed the Chief of Staff in the command of General Djurdjevac in the 4th Corps. Now, as to his own criteria on how the problem in Bosnia should be dealt with, well, I suppose he did, but he could not do anything autonomously or use artillery without the corps command or Djurdjevac knowing. He did not have any links to the paramilitaries either. As far as I know, after the 19th of May, he did not remain and he joined the SDS instead. That's extent of information I have. I think he went back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you mean the VRS or the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, later it became the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Excellencies, I have no further questions of General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, General Vasiljevic. On behalf of this Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the two of us will now leave and another -- another counsel will come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Markovic, I must draw your attention to a particular Rule we have here at the Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering a question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt or saying something that might provide evidence that you have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except for the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kindly pause and speak slowly. Actually, both of us should, so as to make it easier for the interpreters and to have everything in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D07822 in e-court. 1D07822. Aha, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you see that statement of yours on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please give your answer now. The interpretation is over.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. There is a small mistake in number 13. May I correct it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll ask you to do that. Do you have a hard copy of your statement there?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask that the witness be allowed to look at his statement. Could he also be provided with a copy. During the cross-examination he will probably have certain paragraphs quoted to him. Can we now please have paragraph 13 on page 4 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was it that you wanted to correct there? Please tell us what it is that should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that it's Christmas, but I actually spoke about Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 3, it says "over the Catholic Christmas," but it should say "over the Catholic Easter"? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the rest of the statement, does it faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers basically be the same as those provided in this statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this 92 ter ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tendering an associated exhibit? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you would bear with me a minute. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3072, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Mr. Pero Markovic's statement in the English language. [In English] Pero Markovic was elected president of the Executive Board of the Brcko Municipal Assembly. He was involved in the SDS since beginning -- the beginning and was present at the founding Assembly on the 26th of August, 1990. Following the multi-party elections, the Brcko local government was formed from members of the SDA, HDZ, and SDS as a coalition. The Executive Committee of Brcko was composed of nine members, three from each of the parties. Pero Markovic considers that when the Executive Committee was established, it was largely unfit for the purposes or interests of the Serbian people in the municipality. This is because the SDA and HDZ formed a joint front and were able to out-vote the Serbian members of the committee. Therefore, discussions could not be implemented -- decisions could not be implemented that were in the interests of all. The SDS attempted in every way possible to reach a political agreement with the other parties for the benefit of all citizens of the municipality, regardless of religion or nationality. A number of factors had a big impact on the overall inter-ethnic relations in the town, including the civil wars being waged in Slovenia and Croatia because of their immediate proximity to Brcko and that the leaders of the HDZ openly supported the separatist activities in these republics. Further, the SDA in Brcko were under pressure from the SDA leadership from Sarajevo to make personnel changes to allow separatist activities to take place. Mr. Pero Markovic also spoke to a number of Muslim neighbours and friends who were against the demolition of the federal Yugoslavia but were under pressure from the SDA and the HDZ and had to work towards BH seceding. Mr. Pero Markovic was aware that an order was sent from the -- from Jerko Doko, the minister of defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that no mobilisation was to be conducted for the JNA and that the reserve police stations and a police force were to be created. Pero Markovic believes that the reserve police forces and paramilitary units were only formed in towns and neighbourhoods inhabited by Muslims and Croats. This caused the Serb residents in the municipality became anxious and fearful of their safety and put all their hopes in the protection of the JNA. Pero Markovic considers that the symbol of the first rift between the ethnic groups of Brcko was in the SDA and the HDZ tying their party flags together. He was aware that the bridge over the Sava River may be destroyed if the unrest continued. He therefore called a meeting to discuss the possibility of preventing this. However, less than month later, the Croats destroyed their part of bridge. A makeshift bridge was then created. However, this only allowed pedestrians to cross. Further, in April 1992, the Croats stopped pedestrians from crossing the bridge, meaning that between 3.000 and 5.000 people remained in Brcko were unable to return to their home countries from which they had travelled for the holiday. On the night of 29th of April, 1992, Mr. Pero Markovic was awoken by a detonation that discovered -- and discovered that the bridge over the Sava River had been torn down on the right bank of the Sava River. That means on the bank on Bosnian side. The town was gripped by chaos, and the work of the local authorities was paralysed. Mr. Pero Markovic over the radio urged everyone to report to work and remain calm. Mr. Pero Markovic was aware that paramilitary units were mobilising in BH because in March 1992, a large group of well-armed men stopped a JNA column from the local garrison and arrested and disarmed all the JNA members from the column. He called a meeting, and Muslim and Croat leaders confirmed the attack and stated that they would ask their compatriots to release the soldiers, which eventually happened. Pero Markovic therefore concluded that there was collusion between the local government and the paramilitary groups. On 30th of April, 1992, Mr. Pero Markovic was informed that a large group of men fit for military service from Croatia had arrived in the village of Gorica. It was suspected that they were members of the HOS or Green Berets. When questioned, the men stated that they were on holiday. However, Pero Markovic was suspicious as the holiday period was over. On his return to Brcko, Mr. Pero Markovic saw that a barricade had been created -- erected in front of the hospital and was guarded by a number of heavily armed men, the majority of which had automatic weapons. He concluded that these men were members of Muslim paramilitary groups, Patriotic League and the Green Berets. He was also informed that check-points had been set up in the afternoon on all major roads and intersections making it impossible to move around the city. On the afternoon of 1st of May, 1992, members of the Muslim paramilitaries mounted an attack on the town of Brcko, targeting an area inhabited exclusively by Serbs. At the same time paramilitary groups and the HOS were active in Brcko, the JNA withdrew to Serbia and civilian authorities were dysfunctional. This led to the town effectively being ruled by paramilitary groups who made arrests and physically mistreated everyone. These activities made many Serbs fear for their safety. This was amplified when the Serb civilians saw a television broadcast of the massacre of the JNA soldiers. Throughout the war, the town centre and surrounding villages came under indiscriminate gunfire almost every day from Croatia and territory under the control of B and H. That means from north and from south. This shelling caused large-scale destruction of civilian facilities and a large number of civilians who were wounded or killed, and such shelling rendered normal life in the municipality impossible. Serbs, Muslims, and Croats all sought to leave the municipality because of this. Both during and after the war, the Muslim and Croat sides spread numerous lie and told untruths about the war. They misinterpreted [sic] the number of people killed in Brcko as it was publicly stated that more than 8.000 Muslims were killed in Brcko. However, Mr. Pero Markovic is aware that 911 Muslims have been killed in different circumstances. Mr. Pero Markovic had numerous and direct contact with Radovan Karadzic, and throughout he demanded full respect -- Karadzic at that time demanded the full respect for other ethnic groups as well as demanding they represent the interests and welfare of all. Karadzic never asked Pero Markovic to plan or do anything to harm others regardless of their religion or ethnic background. Karadzic asked the authorities to look for solutions for the benefits of everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I wanted to ask you the following: The first time your bridge was destroyed from the Croatian side and the other time it was from the Bosnian side. Was this something new on the Sava or had bridges been destroyed earlier on as well?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, perhaps even a year before that, the bridge between Orasje and Zupanja, near Brcko, had been destroyed. Zupanja is on the Croatian side and Orasje is on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have a document, and perhaps if we have an opportunity, we shall show all the things that had been destroyed up until the 28th of February. But at this point in time, Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Markovic, your evidence in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Markovic. Mr. Markovic, you told us in your statement about the composition of the local government in Brcko before the war. Let me ask you quickly a few -- couple of questions about some other officials in Brcko in that period. Dr. Milenko Vojinovic, also known as Dr. Beli, was president of the SDS in Brcko. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He was also a deputy in the BiH Republican Assembly before the war, later RS Assembly, member of the SDS Main Board, and member of the municipal War Presidency in Brcko. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In his capacity as the president of the municipal SDS and the deputy in the Assembly, he co-ordinated the work of the Municipal Assembly, municipal SDS, pursuant to directions of the SDS leadership in Sarajevo. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Bosko Maricic was vice-president of the SDS Municipal Board, member of the municipal War Presidency, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He became deputy in the RS Assembly in 1995, after the death of Dr. Vojinovic. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic was president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly in Brcko and president of the War Presidency. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Before the war there was a garrison of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, in Brcko. Commander of the garrison was Colonel Pavle Milinkovic. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 7 and 8 of your statement that members of the SDA and HDZ followed instructions from their leadership in Sarajevo and Zagreb. Is it also correct that you followed instructions from the SDS leadership in relation to your activities?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us that the interest of the SDA and the HDZ was independent Bosnia and Herzegovina outside Yugoslavia, which is, you say, against the interest of Serbian people in the municipality of Brcko. At the same time in the discussions with other two parties, the SDS asked for the division of the municipality. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot claim that the SDS asked for that. This idea concerning the division came from us, the parties that were in power, without any instructions from the SDS. If you remember, the Executive Board was three, three, three, so that was the idea of the nine of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear, according to the 1991 census, Serbs made about 20 per cent of the municipal population and about the same number of Brcko town. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There were several meetings held on this topic of division of the municipality, including the one around 17 April 1992 which you referred to in paragraph 33 of your statement. Let me first make it clear. At this time, during these discussions, everyone at these meetings was aware of the situation in Brcko at the time. The war was ongoing in Croatia, Arkan was in Bijeljina, Zvornik, crimes were taking place in Eastern Bosnia, Brcko was packed with refugees and people forced out of their homes trying to cross the bridge in Brcko in order to leave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P03020, page -- English page 5, and B/C/S page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In front of you, Mr. Markovic, there will be a transcript of a TV documentary about Brcko which was produced in Sarajevo. You will be able to see it on the screen, and it's about the negotiations that -- that you talk about in your statement. Mato Jurisic, a Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So English page 5; B/C/S, 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you -- you can look at the screen. It says here MJ, that's Mato Jurisic, a Croat, he refers to the committee that you also talk about in paragraph 33. Munib Jusufovic says that he did not want any division. Mustafa Ramic said that the SDS wanted to divide town into two parts. Ibrahim Ramic said three-quarters of the town would have belonged to the Serbs, the entire industrial area, the railway, and the harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page in English and B/C/S. He says that -- okay. Can we have in B/C/S next page? Ibrahim Ramic, that the other two communities did not consider this to be a serious proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Was this, Mr. Markovic, a general position of the parties during these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You've put many questions. If we are talking about the division, we tried in a way to do our best to prevent a war, all three sides. Unfortunately, this never came to pass. I already talked about that. We had this Municipal Assembly session that was broadcast on local TV and that was the reason. We just didn't want any kind of conflict to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the only other question I want to ask about this, if you look at the screen it says Vinko Marjanovic, he says -- you can see "VM." You can read that. According to him -- yeah, you can read that.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: According to him -- Vinko Marjanovic was a Croat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: According to him, at some point he had discussion with you and you told him that peace would not prevail regardless of the outcome of the negotiations. Did you say this to Mr. Vinko Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In the morning hours of 30th April 1992, at 4.50, the bridges across the Sava River were blown up and this was practically the beginning of the war in Brcko municipality. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement, paragraph 31, that you were in Stanovi in the first week of May 1992. When exactly did you go to Stanovi, and when did you return to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, I left, and I'm not sure when it was that I returned, possibly on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic testifies -- testified that the day before the bridges were blown up, the garrison commander warned him to move to Stanovi for safety reasons and to bring other War Presidency members with him. This is in P03023, page 18. Did you go, Mr. Markovic, to Stanovi with this group of people?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My parents lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic also testified that the War Presidency returned to Brcko on 4 May 1992 and that it was initially placed in the building called Sumadija in the Bijeljinska Street, which was the head the forest company. This is at transcript page 16710. He said that there were discussions about future executive government after 6 May 1992, and according to him, you did not want to continue performing this position. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If it matters, the building is Sumarija, not Sumadija. It really does matter in our language. I don't know whether it matters in English too. Sumarija means forestry building because it was a forestry company. As for the take-over of power since that kind of chaos prevailed, hardly anyone would want to play any role in government at that point in time, myself included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The War Presidency had meetings from early May 1992, and it was in charge of issuing passes for moving, public services, and other issues related to the functioning of the local government. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we tried to pretend we were a government. There was no water, electricity. Somebody had to try at least to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 17268.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In front of you, Mr. Markovic, there will be a travel permit issued by the Brcko War Presidency on the basis of the decision of the War Presidency of 3 May 1992. The heading of the document, it has information about the new Serb authorities in Brcko. English version says that the heading is illegible, but you can look at the stamp, Mr. Markovic, and there's a signature of Djordje Ristanic. Mr. Markovic, the local authorities resumed their work in Brcko shortly after the take-over operations had begun. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no one to take it over from. By the 30th of April, we had normal government, and after that none whatsoever. So there was no one to take it over from. If I properly understood the interpretation of what you said. You said took over the power, but there was no one to take it over from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: What I meant is before 30th April 1992, it was, let's call it a joint government in Brcko, and after 30th April 1992, as we can see in this document, it's a Serb municipality of Brcko. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, but there was no take-over as you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think the witness has really said anything about the document that would cause it to be admitted through his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness's evidence was that -- and I believe he said middle May there was no government. Here this document shows that there was a government before middle May, and they were functioning. So this is classic impeachment document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did he confirm that it is a governmental document? All you said is "illegible." Did he confirm the signature of Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, if you look at the document, can you confirm the signature? Is that Djordje Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that it is Djordje Ristanic's signature, but the date which is in the upper part of the document is the 8th rather than the 4th, as I believe you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I did not say 4, but, yeah, thank you. And also if you look the stamp, this is the stamp that the new Serb government or authorities in Brcko used after 30th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I oppose your claim that there was a taking over of power. There was no power at all, and I said that we were trying to establish some sort of power. If you have a situation in which nothing is functioning, then it's normal to attempt to establish some kind of authority and power. So this could have been an attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, did you want to take a break or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break now for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just take this moment, please, to introduce Ms. Marija Grujeska, who has been working in our Belgrade office for almost a year now, and she is not going to make a long speech, I assure you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zec, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the Brcko garrison and Lieutenant-Colonel Pavle Milinkovic remained in Brcko during and after the take-over of the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you keep using this term "take-over."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that Pavle Milinkovic remained in the city in this period?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have quickly D01577.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In front of you there will be a travel permit issued by the commander of the Brcko garrison, Lieutenant-Colonel Pavle Milinkovic on 8th July 1992, and in paragraph 20, you say that it moved to Serbia in May 1992. So that's -- I'm asking this question. So it is clear, isn't it, that Pavle Milinkovic remained in Brcko during this period?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no signature here but a facsimile on this pass. The JNA left Brcko on May 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I asked you and you said yes. I asked you whether Pavle Milinkovic and Brcko garrison remained in Brcko just a moment ago and you said yes. And this is basically confirmation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until May 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milinkovic and the garrison as the garrison could not walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do not interrupt while the witness is saying something, Mr. Karadzic, please. What did you say, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the JNA left Brcko on May 19. I have no information as to when exactly Pavle Milinkovic crossed the border. I believe he did that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the previous set of conversation, you confirmed that Mr. Milinkovic stayed in Brcko at this time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until May 19. I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What was your point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my objection was about confusing questions that say during the take-over and during and after the take-over whether the JNA and the garrison left. How can a garrison leave? So just to simplify questions. The JNA left on the 19th, but the garrison didn't leave. It didn't go anywhere. And thirdly, do we have confirmation that this is Milinkovic's signature? It is typed, but do we have a signature as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not an appropriate intervention, Mr. Karadzic, at all, the last point. Yes, back to you, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but if you look the date of this document, it's July 1992. So he was there way after May 1992. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: MUP of Serb republic regulated the movement in Brcko by issuing passes for movement. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This pass was issued by the garrison command rather than by the MUP, if this is the one you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, it's not. This was my question. Can you confirm? I'll show you another document, but can you confirm that the MUP of Serb republic was regulating movement in the city by issuing documents such as this one?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the passes were issued by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24668.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In front of you there will be a travel permit that has the same format as the one that's been seen a moment ago. And this permit has the stamp of the MUP of Serb republic on it for which you say in paragraph 20 of your statement there was powerful [sic] to do anything. So can you have a look at the stamp and confirm this is the stamp of the MUP of Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but at the time anyone could make a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is the stamp of the MUP of Serb republic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Registrar, we could blow-up the area that -- this area where the stamp is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says down there commander Lieutenant-Colonel Pavle Milinkovic. He is a soldier and the stamp is from the police, as the gentleman claims. And in the heading it also says "Garrison," Brcko garrison. So it's the army once again. So one of them is too many. One of them is surplus; right? I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When I introduced this document to you, I said it uses the same format as the one that we saw signed by Milinkovic, but this one has stamp of the MUP of Serb republic and has no Milinkovic signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6173.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, a unit under command of Zika Ivanovic or Zika Crnogorac was in Brcko during this period, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He also issued passes for movement, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have quickly D01578. I'll move on. I won't use this. This is already in evidence. Can we have P03026.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the War Presidency issued passes for people they believed should be released from Luka camp, and those passes were provided to Goran Jelisic. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P03026.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In front of you there will be a pass issued by the War Presidency on 14 May 1992. It has the same format as the one we saw earlier, but this was -- this one was signed by Adolf. This Chamber -- sorry, this is Goran Jelisic, who called himself the Serb Adolf Hitler. Djordje Ristanic testified that the War Presidency gave these passes to Jelisic for people they believed should be released from Luka. Transcript page 16 -- 16718. Mr. Markovic, this was a way of co-ordination between Goran Jelisic and the War Presidency. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Goran Jelisic was never a member of the War Presidency. Up until those days he was a completely unknown person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I did not suggest that he was member of the War Presidency. He was in Luka camp, and I said that War Presidency, when they believed one should be released from the Luka camp, they would provide these passes such as this one to Goran Jelisic in the Luka camp to release people. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You may be partly right. The passes were used by everyone, whoever wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's not my question. War Presidency provided passes to Goran Jelisic if they believed one should be released from Luka camp, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer like that. It's possible that Ristanic personally gave it to him, but officially no one ever gave it to him at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16, it's not recorded that the witness said "not only those from Luka." So whoever wanted to leave, not only those from Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can I move on, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you told us in your statement in paragraph 9 that the Serbs had put all their hopes for protection in the units of the JNA garrison in Brcko. This Chamber has received evidence that Serbs in Brcko believed that the forces within Brcko were not sufficient to take control of the municipality. The SDS asked for assistance from Bijeljina, which was part of the same region, SAO Semberija and Majevica. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you are saying the SDS. It wasn't just the SDS, if I understood you well, or maybe it's a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My question was that the SDS asked assistance from Bijeljina. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency asked for that rather than the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I refer to transcript page 16711 and P00956, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, as a result of this request, various Serb forces came to Brcko, mainly from Bijeljina, to assist the take-over of town. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help me, because you said "various Serb forces." What exactly did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will be asking you about specific units that came. So can you confirm that Serb forces came?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The first Serbian force that arrived to Brcko about four to six months before the war was the group of instructors of Captain Dragan, the Red Berets or Knindzas as they called them at the time. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among this group of Captain Dragan instructors there was Rade and Bozo Bozic, Simo Radovanovic, Sasa Vukojevic, Goran Petkovic, and others. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about some of those names but I don't know when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: They arrived and formed a special unit which provided trainings for Brcko residents. This was one of the first Serbian forces in Brcko; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in P02888, English page 3, B/C/S e-court page 9. And in D01412, English page 7, B/C/S page 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The largest -- Mr. Markovic, the largest part of the Serbian forces that came to Brcko was from the area of Semberija. That is from Bijeljina and Ugljevik. Those were Serbian guards under the command of Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer, and a unit of radicals under the command of Mirko Blagojevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Those units were present in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Branislav Filipovic, also known as Sumar, was among the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party that took part in the take-over of Brcko. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of name Branislav Filipovic, also known as Sumar?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that the command of the Brcko garrison authorised Branislav Filipovic to bring weapons from Belgrade for the needs of the Brcko garrison. This is in P02877. They also gave him a vehicle for his trips to Belgrade and Bijeljina in May 1992. This is in P02902. There's also a receipt issued to Branislav Filipovic in Belgrade for the weapons he took for the needs of the Brcko garrison. This is in P02876. Mr. Markovic, the Brcko War Presidency issued Sumar or Branislav Filipovic a pass to travel out of the war zone and Brcko municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but the War Presidency met very rarely. It is possible that someone from the War Presidency issued this pass and gave it to him, but this is not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P0874 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in front of you there will be a pass issued by the Brcko War Presidency. This pass was issued to Branislav Filipovic to be able to go out of the battle zone in Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, if you -- if you look at this pass, can you see name of Branislav Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the last name, and I suppose that it is the corresponding first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It says also that there's a note that Sumar was a volunteer from Bijeljina, but if you look the signature, do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's completely illegible. It's completely illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have the reverse side of this document. There is second page. Mr. Registrar, can you also turn for the witness to be able to see this handwriting. Can you turn it around?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this handwriting, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I can read out the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic, Pero Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This refers to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Is it then possible that Sumar made a note of these two names on his pass?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among the units -- I asked you a moment ago about Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer, and you confirmed that he was present in Bijeljina. Is it also correct that he came to Bijeljina on 2nd May of 1992? I'm sorry, not Bijeljina, Brcko.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that he arrived on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 45341B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It is correct, isn't it, Mr. Markovic, that Mauzer made agreement with the command of the garrison at the time with the Presidency of the municipal -- Serbian municipal -- municipality of Brcko for him to arrive to Brcko? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that there was an agreement, but I wasn't privy to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have also B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the beginning it says -- this is -- Mr. Markovic, this is Mauzer speaking. This is the documentary of the unit under Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer. And he's talking here about his arrival to Brcko, and in the first line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that there's no B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Oversight, but it should be available somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the translation for English and B/C/S exists in the form of audio recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So we have tape which is transcribed in B/C/S and then translated in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can also play, but I believe we spend a lot of time if I play the video, so we will be able to find transcript very quickly. I'll come back to this in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you said that Zika Ivanovic, also known as Zika Crnogorac, was in Brcko. He led a unit of the Serbian MUP of Red Berets. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 15117.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in front of you there will be a certificate issued by the MUP of Serbia, unit for special purposes, dated 27 June 1992. Signature, commander of the unit, Zika Ivanovic. This is Zika Ivanovic, commander of the Red Berets that came to Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the man's name, but I am aware of Zika Crnogorac if this is the person in question. Otherwise, I don't know what his first and last name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Zika Ivanovic, nickname is Zika Crnogorac; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's no basis for this through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, what witness confirmed is name. What would you respond to Mr. Robinson's observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He confirmed that the unit commanded by Zika Ivanovic or Zika Crnogorac came to Brcko and this is certificate to show that he was -- that he was member of the Serbian MUP, and he's signing this document as the commander of special purposes unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness did not identify the person whose name appears on this document as being the same as the one that Mr. Zec is representing it to be. He just said "fine," meaning he agrees with -- meaning whatever you say, whatever, but he didn't say that he knew that this man whose name appears on this document is the same one that they had been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I first asked -- I'm sorry. When I first asked about Zika Ivanovic and his presence in Brcko, the witness said yes, I believe, earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question is what the witness confirmed about this document. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, the Chamber would not receive this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 15118.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in front of you there will be another certificate issued by Zika Ivanovic. This time he entitles his unit as a unit for special purposes Brcko under SAO Semberija and Majevica. This certificate was -- is dated 9 July 1992, confirming that Joco Stevanovic is a member of this unit from 20 June 1992. Zika said we need every man, especially a sniper. Zika ends with words "in co-operation of MUP Krajina with the units of SAO Semberija and Majevica." Mr. Markovic, this is the unit under Zika Ivanovic that came to Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that units from MUP Krajina, Semberija and Majevica were present in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I may assist. In line 24, page 84, the witness said, "I don't know what his real name is, but I did hear of a Zika Crnogorac." Page 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, should we take a different action from the one we saw before, 15117?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if I show another document to show that Zika Ivanovic is Zika Crnogorac, maybe then it will be clear as to who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: P02855. Can we have next page in both languages. So English page I'm looking is 5. In English -- in English, that's second-last paragraph. Can we have B/C/S next page. I'm sorry, back. Previous page. I'm trying to find the same quote basically. Sorry, the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, if you look at third paragraph from the top, it says: "Krajina Special Police with 45 men led by Zivojin Ivanovic, also known as Crnogorac ..." Mr. Markovic, this is -- this is Zivojin Ivanovic, also known as Zika Crnogorac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender the previous document, which was 65 ter 15118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think this previous document as well as the one before it can be admitted with this link. Even though the witness didn't confirm anything about the document, it might be considered sufficiently contradictory to be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, given the circumstances, the Chamber will admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6174 and 6175 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I would like to play a video-clip, which is P02852, and I would like to play second clip which starts from time-code 00:09:02 of the tape V000-3533. This is a celebration ceremony of the Red Berets unit of the Serbian state security in 1997 in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can stop. Perhaps while we're waiting I can now call 65 ter 25341B. Mr. President, I believe we have now the video that I intended to play a moment ago, which is P02852, which is a celebration ceremony of the Red Berets. So we can start.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you hear the interpreter's comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I believe should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot see e-court independently in the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can play without translation. I'm only interested that the witness hears the name of people, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can stop, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, did you hear the name at the beginning of this clip?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's Zika Ivanovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the name that was pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This was Zika Ivanovic who was assisting the take-over of Brcko. Here we see him saluting the unit accompanied by Slobodan Milosevic and Jovica Stanisic from the Serbian State Security. The reality is, Mr. Markovic, there was no confusion as to what was the task of these units in Brcko during the take-over and who was behind them. All these units had one task, to make Brcko Serbian, which they accomplished very fast. It was only after the take-over was accomplished and Muslims had been detained or expelled, only then did these units cause difficulties for the Serbian authorities in Brcko. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just go back -- would like to go back to the document that I was trying to upload, and there was no B/C/S translation, which was 65 ter 45341B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the 65 ter number of the video-clip that we just saw? You said 25341B. Is there a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The clip that we saw is P02852, and this clip starts from 00:09:02 of the video-tape V000-0533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in front of you is a transcript of the video interview of Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer. And when I asked you earlier about his arrival to Brcko on 2nd May 1992, he said, and you confirmed that, as I believe. And you can see now at the beginning of this transcript that he's saying that he came on 2nd May 1992 to Brcko. This is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I notice that the transcript refers to an unidentified male person and doesn't make any reference to Mauzer. Perhaps there's some other way of establishing that, but I don't see how this witness can be asked to comment on the statement of Mauzer when we don't have a foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Then we can upload the video and see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention, please. The witness did not confirm anything. He simply allowed for the possibility that Mauzer arrived on the 2nd. He said it was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's see what witness will say about this video footage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you recognise person on this frame?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Does this satisfy, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the transcript that we saw is a transcription of this video that we are seeing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. President, that's documentary about Ljubisa Savic Mauzer unit, and it goes chronologically from their establishment throughout the war, all their operations, and it's accompanying various video-clips about their activities, and that's Mauzer speaking about the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So I believe it will be now easier if we go back to the transcript and just see a few portions of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will that be your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Markovic, I asked you about agreement with Mauzer with the local authorities, and you said, "I believe that's possible" or something like that. So if you look at the transcript, in English it's at line 11 -- from line 11, and in B/C/S line 29. Can you read, Mr. Markovic? "Mauzer said the agreement with the command at the time with the Presidency of the Serbian municipality of Brcko was that help would arrive to Brcko from Semberija the following day. When we returned from Brcko, we called all Crisis Staffs in Semberija - there were 54 of them - asking them to send volunteers. Some 700 of us headed out." This is how Mauzer came to Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there were 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But can you confirm that this was the way how he arrived to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he arrived in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When I earlier asked you the same question, you said "possible," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible. Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the reason he came to Brcko was because Brcko had to be Serbian. It was a hub. It was an umbilical cord, a connection between the -- a connection and a link between eastern Serbian Krajinas, so to say, Serbian lands. This is the reason why he came to Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea what this has to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look -- if you look the same page or in English it's from line 28.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did not find its way in the transcript is the witness said, "I don't know what Luka has to do with it."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S can we move to see the -- so it's line 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you see when he says at that Brcko was a connection, link between eastern Serbian Krajinas and Serbian lands? So that's the reason he came to Brcko, because Brcko had to become Serbian for this reason, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see why it would be that way. He arrived in Brcko that, if we're going to put it that way, already had been Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is a third-party statement after the fact. It hasn't been confirmed at all by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I don't think that he did not confirm anything. The witness was saying "possible," and this was happening. It's not that he didn't say it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, the Chamber finds that what -- the testimony of this witness is a bit short of confirmation of the content of this video, so we'll not admit this at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, just a few matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Markovic, on page 88 of today's transcript, the following was suggested to you, the following order of events or sequence of events. It seems that first that Zika Crnogorac took Brcko, and then Muslims were either detained or expelled. Can you shed more light on the actual sequence of events? When did Muslims leave the Serb part of Brcko, and what does this have to do with Zika Crnogorac's arrival?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the arrival of Zika Crnogorac. As far as I can remember, he arrived in July or in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did the Muslims leave, as well as Serbs, from the central part of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already explained that. The destruction of the bridge on the right bank of the Sava River was the point when practically the entire population left the town of Brcko - Serb, Croats, and Muslims - and that basically it was an empty town for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today it was often suggested to you that there was a take-over of power in Brcko. Can you please tell us who was it was that was in power in Brcko before these events and after these events?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was the representative of the authorities until the destruction of the bridges. I was the president of the Executive Board, and also there was a Muslim who was president of the municipality and so on and so forth. So it was according to this ethnic key that the various offices in the municipality were divided, and in mid-May, a government was reinstated, and there was a man who was appointed whose last name was also Markovic, but that wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see "Serb municipality of Brcko" in some of the letterheads. Can you explain to us what it was that you held under your control and what was meant by the Serb municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already explained that. I said today that we had discussions on the territorial division of town, and in Brcko, it was possible to divide most of the territory along ethnic lines because the villages have a majority population belonging to one particular group. Also, it was possible to divide the town itself in a similar way. For example, there is a part of town that's called Serb Town, and then it continues along into the, say, Serb villages, and the situation is similar on the two other sides as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How old is this, this Serb Town? What's the oldest part of the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that's the oldest part of town. I don't know how old it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serb municipality of Brcko, did it control the Muslim municipality of Brcko or the Croat municipality of Brcko, and who was in power there?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, throughout the war there were practically three municipalities of Brcko. One was under the control of the Serbs and another one was under Muslim control. I think it was called "free Brcko." And then there was one that was under the control of Croats, and it was called the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what it was called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the territory of Brcko was controlled in that way if we look at the inner city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ravne Brcko. Could you please speak a bit slower. We do have time.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Ravne Brcko. That was the part of the municipality that was under the control of the Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the Muslim municipality of Brcko and the Croat municipality of Brcko? Was there a change of government there as well? Who was in power there?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was in power there. Over the local radio that was called Free Radio Brcko, I could hear that it was those people who had been together with me in the local government. Some of them were mentioned here today as well. They were in the local government together with me before the destruction of the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6175, could I call that up, please. We had it admitted a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, in Markovic, do you know who General Tolimir is?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard of General Tolimir. Now, I don't know who he is. I mean, I think he was a high-ranking officer of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation So this seems to be the other way round. Give us the other one, the 74 or the 76. Oh, not, not this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, now that we're on this one, tell us, is there a stamp here, and is there a registration number?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you worked in the state administration, would you consider this to be an official document?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have Tolimir's text, P6174. That's what I wrote down. Maybe it's 76 too. They were admitted as a series, so I don't know which number was assigned to which one of them. 74, then. No, no. Sorry, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. Zec. The last page in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This gentleman, General Tolimir, who did he work for? He was a colonel then, a general now. Was he in the Army of Republika Srpska? What state was he in?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, in the third paragraph from the top of the page where he speaks about Zika Crnogorac in Brcko, what is his position vis-a-vis Zika Crnogorac?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you take a look at the penultimate paragraph? Actually, you can read it out loud to us.

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: "The presence and activity of paramilitary formations negatively affect the Serbian people in two ways, by diminishing trust in the government and its capacity to deal with war profiteers, criminals, and mass murderers, and secondly, by immensely discouraging the fighting along of the members of the army of the SRBH often resulting in the abandoning of positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you know that this text was written by Tolimir about the paramilitary formations, can you tell us now what the position of this General of the Army of Republika Srpska is vis-a-vis --

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does it say here that the government does not have the strength or that the government does not want to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I asked these questions the witness did not know anything and he said doesn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, what was the position and attitude of the authorities vis-a-vis Zika Crnogorac and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We tried to get rid of them in every conceivable way, and we asked the leadership of Republika Srpska for assistance and also from the army, whoever could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the strength to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's why we asked for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you actually deal with them and in what situation?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-July, I think, something like that. A unit came under the command of Mico Davidovic. I think that it was sent from the MUP of Republika Srpska with that intention. It was only that unit that managed to drive them out of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see P2888.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 71, you were asked about the War Presidency and about them signing something. Now, this is what I'm asking you: The War Presidency at the time, could it implement any decision of its own?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was virtually impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a summary of events and situations, and we can see that on the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the penultimate page please be shown to -- actually, the participants can see for themselves the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is this, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on the back of that ID where it says "Ristanic Djordje" and "Markovic Pero," are those your signatures?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, please, could we have page 2 in English and page 4 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did the Presidency establish or support any one of those paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the penultimate paragraph. "The policy of the Serb leadership of the municipal War Presidency was that all conscripts had to be placed under the command of the Brcko garrison immediately."

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's changed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please return the previous page. It is 4 in e-court and it says 3 on the page itself. In English it's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So under the command of Colonel Milinkovic and that all war operations would be commanded by, et cetera, et cetera, the Serb population did not for one moment form any paramilitary formations. How does this fit into your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I said in my statement that all our eyes were focused on the JNA then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was your military-age population, under whose command?

utterances.speaker: PERO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA, later the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have page 8 in e-court in Serbian, and page 4 and then later on page 5. Actually, first page 4 in English. Eight in e-court, Serbian. Actually, it says 7 on it. Page 4 in e-court. What is written is 7, but it's the eighth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read it out until it is here. This primarily refers to Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer; Mirko Blagojevic; Sasa and Peja; Arkan's volunteers; and instructors, Captain Dragan special unit.
